title: Payments Webhook Service
summary: Idempotent webhook receiver for a lending platform: signature verification, deduplication, and retry with backoff. Processes millions of events daily without duplicate ledger entries.
problem: Customers were double-posted to the ledger whenever a payment retried — the gateway replays the same webhook and our handler treated it as a new payment.

rationale.why: The gateway's retry behaviour is out of our control, so correctness had to live on our side of the boundary.

decisions.reason: High-concurrency handlers with low memory and a single static binary — small, cheap containers.
Events had to be replayable for backfills, not just consumed once from a queue.
Deduplication enforced by the database, not application logic — far harder to get wrong.

impact: Zero duplicate ledger entries since release, ~2M events per day, and a lighter worker fleet that cut infrastructure cost.

title: API Gateway Rate Limiter
summary: Sliding-window rate limiter middleware backed by Redis, with per-tenant quotas and clear 429 responses.
problem: One noisy tenant could exhaust the shared API and slow everyone else down; there was no per-client limit at all.

rationale.why: We needed enforcement in milliseconds at the edge, without adding another database to operate.

decisions.reason: Lived inside the existing gateway process — no new deploy target, reused the team's tooling.
Atomic counters shared across gateway instances; in-memory limits would be wrong behind a load balancer.

impact: Removed the noisy-neighbour incidents entirely and turned opaque 500s into explicit 429s that clients can handle.

title: Job Queue Worker
summary: Celery worker setup for image processing and report generation, with per-queue concurrency and dead-letter handling.
problem: Image resizing and report generation ran inside request handlers, so slow jobs blocked users and reports were hours late.

rationale.why: Work was bursty and unequal — a report could take minutes while a thumbnail took a second.

decisions.reason: The image and report libraries we already depended on were Python; no reason to rewrite the logic.
Per-queue concurrency let slow report jobs run separately from fast image jobs.
Reliable acknowledgements and a dead-letter path for jobs that fail repeatedly.

impact: Report delay dropped from ~12 hours to minutes and API response times no longer depend on the heaviest workload.

title: Inventory REST API
summary: Spring Boot inventory service with optimistic locking, stock reservations, and OpenAPI documentation.
problem: Warehouse staff oversold items because two checkouts could decrement the same stock row at the same time.

rationale.why: The service is owned by a Java team and will be maintained by them after I moved on.

decisions.reason: Matched the team's existing skills — handover mattered more than my own language preference.
Contention is low; retrying a version conflict is cheaper than locking every read.
The mobile team integrates directly; generated docs removed back-and-forth.

impact: Overselling stopped, and the API is still maintained by the team without my involvement.
